blocks.md: An LSM tree turns random writes into sequential runs. The price is paid later: reads may search several overlapping runs, while compaction rewrites data to reduce that search.

blocks.label: FIG 1
blocks.caption: Waiting creates more Level-0 overlap and read work. Compacting too eagerly rewrites data repeatedly and stalls the write path.

blocks.title: Plans must be overlap-closed
blocks.md: Once you select a Level-0 key range, include every Level-1 run that overlaps it. Omitting one can leave two versions of a key in places the read rules cannot reconcile.

blocks.input:
L0 A: keys [10, 30]
L0 B: keys [25, 50]
L1 X: keys [0, 20]
L1 Y: keys [40, 60]
blocks.output: selecting A + B also requires X + Y
blocks.explain: The chosen Level-0 union spans keys 10 through 50. Both Level-1 runs intersect that range, so both belong in the merge even though neither overlaps every selected Level-0 run.

items: Every plan targets Level 1 and includes at least one existing Level-0 run.
Include all and only the Level-1 runs overlapping the selected Level-0 range.
Keep the newest entry for each key; tombstones participate in recency.
Return no work below your trigger instead of emitting an empty or stale plan.

items.title: Start at the published trigger
items.md: Compacting all Level-0 runs is a correct baseline and establishes overlap handling.

items.title: Price the candidate
items.md: Estimate bytes rewritten and the read overlap removed by each valid input set.

items.title: Avoid tiny repeated merges
items.md: A cheap compaction now may rewrite the same key range again after the next flush.

blocks.title: The four-way trade-off
blocks.md: Read amplification, bytes rewritten, compaction stalls, and peak disk space pull in different directions. A useful policy makes that trade explicit instead of optimizing a single counter.
